one_liner: Strict Rust HTTP/1.1 parser (crate, C++ lib, WASM) meant to replace llhttp in Node.js; ~1.07x llhttp in one test.
what_it_does: Parses HTTP/1.1 requests and responses incrementally and reports spans (offset, length) for the method, URL, headers, body data, chunk extensions and trailers. It delivers them through callbacks or through a parser-owned binary event buffer. It ships as the milo-parser crate (which also installs a CLI), a C++ header plus libmilo.a, and an npm WebAssembly package (@perseveranza-pets/milo, SIMD and no-SIMD builds). The API has the same shape as llhttp (create/parse/pause/resume/finish, span callbacks) but is not source- or behaviour-compatible: names, flags and error codes differ, and it rejects input that llhttp accepts.
how_it_is_fast: It is a line-oriented state machine. Proc-macros (syn/quote) generate its states, matchers and byte lookup tables (token, request-target, quoted-string) at compile time. CR and separators are found with memchr/memchr2. Header lines are scanned 16 bytes at a time for CR and invalid control bytes, using SSE2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64 and simd128 on wasm32, with a scalar fallback. The parser reports offsets into the caller's buffer instead of copying data; the one copy is an optional re-buffering of unconsumed input (manage_unconsumed). Since 0.8.0 events go to a 64 KiB per-parser buffer and callbacks are replayed from it at the end of parse().
when_to_use: You want to embed a strict HTTP/1.1-only parser in Rust, C++ or JS/WASM, and rejecting obs-fold, bare LF/CR, HTTP/1.0, duplicate Content-Length, CL+TE together and GET/HEAD bodies is what you want (request-smuggling hardening).
You build natively (not WASM) and want a span/callback parser like llhttp, written in readable Rust instead of llparse-generated C.
You are evaluating the parser its author proposes as llhttp's successor in Node.js and can run the repo's benchmarks/cpp or benchmarks/wasm harness on your own hardware first.
when_not_to_use: Node.js/undici-style WASM deployments where speed is the reason to switch: the author's own 2023 deck says milo is slower than llhttp when compiled to WebAssembly, and no newer WASM numbers are published.
Servers that must accept HTTP/1.0 clients, RTSP, obs-fold or bare-LF peers. Milo rejects all of these by design and does not aim for llhttp behavioural compatibility.

Untrusted production traffic without your own fuzzing. Two fuzzing reports from 2026-06-08 are still open: #15, a memory leak on invalid input, and #16, OOM on malformed headers. The 0.x API also changed in five releases in June 2026.
Servers holding many idle connections: each parser allocates a 64 KiB event buffer, whereas the README describes the parser state as only a few dozen fields.
You only need an llhttp speedup you can verify: the single published comparison is a 7% gain within noise, from a 2023 build that predates the 2026 SIMD rewrite.

integration.form: crate (milo-parser) | static lib + header (libmilo.a, milo.h) | npm WASM module
integration.dependencies: memchr (runtime). Building the C++/WASM artifacts also needs cargo-make, cbindgen, the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and Binaryen wasm-opt.
integration.min_toolchain: The repo pins nightly Rust (rust-toolchain.toml; the C++/WASM tasks use -Z flags; PR #17 to build on stable is open). The crate is edition 2024 with no declared rust-version. C++ consumers compile with -std=c++11. The npm package needs Node >= 22.21.0.
integration.platforms: any Rust target; hand-written SIMD paths for x86-64 (SSE2), aarch64 (NEON) and wasm32 (simd128), scalar fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. A Parser is a mutable #[repr(C)] struct holding raw pointers (context, events, unconsumed), so use one parser per connection and do not share it across threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same callback-and-span model as llhttp, but different API names, error codes and flags, stricter acceptance rules, the caller must set skip_body for responses to HEAD, and there is no llhttp compatibility shim

gotchas: An incomplete line is left unconsumed: parse() returns fewer bytes than it was given. With manage_unconsumed on, milo copies the leftover bytes and prepends them on the next call. Reading parse.rs, the retained buffer is created with Vec::into_raw_parts and only rebuilt as a slice with from_raw_parts afterwards, which does not free it, so this mode appears to leak on every partial parse.
When the 64 KiB event buffer fills, parse() stops early without an error or pause; the caller must drain events and call parse() again.
Responses to HEAD require the caller to set skip_body; milo does not pair requests with responses. CONNECT responses likewise need application context.
WASM release builds use immediate-abort panics, so a panic traps with no message; the debug build is needed to diagnose errors.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick milo over iohttpparser when you need Rust, C++ and WASM builds from one strict codebase aimed at Node.js; iohttpparser has much stronger published evidence against llhttp (median req/s over 22 scenarios). zttp and gunicorn_h1c are only relevant if you are in Python.
verified_claims_summary: The only comparison is one autocannon run (11 one-second samples) against a Node.js native-addon HTTP server, shown in the author's NodeConf EU 2023 deck: milo averaged 30,765 req/s vs 28,808 req/s for llhttp (about 1.07x, with stdev about 1.4k req/s for each). The deck gives no CPU, OS, compiler, flags or harness. The repo's current C++ harness (clang -O3 -march=native -flto for llhttp v9.3.1, target-cpu=native for milo, no callbacks enabled on either) and its WASM harness (vs undici's llhttp_simd.wasm) publish no results.
status_note: Actively developed and ISC-licensed; v0.8.0 shipped 2026-06-25. Adoption is small (219 crates.io downloads in total, about 8k npm downloads in the last month) and GitHub issue search found no milo issues in nodejs/undici or the nodejs org. Treat it as pre-1.0 and experimental.
